claims.text: The proposed alloy has titanium and nickel as its primary constituents, each at approximately 30–40 at%, with at least three additional elements each at 5–35 at%.
The proposed composition satisfies the stated high-entropy-alloy compositional criteria.
Aging at approximately 800°C for 4 hours will induce Ni3Ti or a similar ordered phase in the alloy.
The aging treatment will produce evenly dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
The induced Ni3Ti or similar precipitates will remain thermally stable under elevated-temperature testing or service.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede dislocation motion.
The nanoscale precipitates will impede grain-boundary sliding.
Impeding dislocation motion will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
Impeding dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding will slow elevated-temperature creep deformation.
At approximately 700°C, the aged alloy will have greater yield strength than the otherwise identical unaged alloy.
At approximately 700°C, the aged alloy will have better creep resistance than the otherwise identical unaged alloy.
Four hours of aging is sufficient to encourage nanoscale precipitation without excessive precipitate coarsening.
An 800°C aging temperature and a 700°C testing temperature are appropriate boundaries for this alloy and application.
A yield-strength improvement below 10% is insufficient to support the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state example permits titanium and nickel concentrations up to about 40 at%, whereas the boundary requires every constituent to remain at or below 35 at%.

The predicted outcome claims an unspecified increase in yield strength, but the falsification rule rejects increases below 10%; thus a positive increase could satisfy the stated prediction while simultaneously falsifying it.
